Vignette: Priya, Age 22

Priya grew up in a close-knit South Asian household where the expectation was simple: work hard, stay safe, take care of your family. At nineteen she started driving deliveries to help with household expenses, and for two years the job suited her - she liked the solitude of the road, the sense of being useful, the small pride of knowing her way around the city better than most people her age. Then, on a Tuesday evening in November, everything changed.

She had just completed a drop-off in an unfamiliar part of the city when two men approached her at her car. One grabbed her arm. The other pressed something cold and hard against her ribs and told her not to make a sound. They took her phone, her wallet, her car keys, and the delivery bag still warm from the restaurant. The whole thing lasted less than three minutes. She stood on the pavement in the dark for what felt like a very long time afterward, unable to move, unable to call out, her body simply refusing to cooperate.

That was eight months ago. Priya tells the story now in a flat, measured voice, as though recounting something that happened to someone else - but her hands grip the hem of her jacket the entire time she speaks.

She went back to driving within two weeks because the bills did not pause for her fear. She tells herself this was the right decision. In practice, it means she spends six to eight hours a day in conditions that feel almost unbearable. Every time she parks in a poorly lit street she scans every shadow before she opens the door. She keeps the engine running longer than she needs to. She has rerouted deliveries to avoid the neighbourhood where the robbery happened, adding twenty minutes to some runs, and she has not told her dispatcher why. When a car pulls up beside her at a red light and the driver glances over, her heart slams against her chest and she grips the steering wheel until her knuckles pale.

Sleep is its own problem. She lies awake replaying the moment the cold object touched her side, trying to think her way to a different ending - one where she fought back, or ran, or said something. She cannot find that ending. When she does sleep she wakes from dreams she cannot always remember, only the feeling of being pinned, of her voice not working. She is exhausted in a way that rest does not seem to touch.

At home she is quieter than she used to be. Her mother notices and asks questions Priya does not know how to answer. Saying I was robbed feels both accurate and completely inadequate, and she worries that if she explains the full weight of it her family will insist she quit the job, which she cannot afford to do. She has told no one the part about the object pressed to her ribs. She is not entirely sure why. Partly shame, partly the fear that saying it aloud will make it more real than it already is.

She finds herself irritable in ways that surprise her - snapping at her younger brother over small things, then feeling a wash of guilt so heavy it is almost physical. She has stopped meeting friends on weekends, telling them she is tired from work, which is true but is not the whole truth. The whole truth is that crowded spaces make her feel cornered, and noise that comes from behind her makes her flinch, and she no longer fully trusts her own ability to read a situation as safe.

What Priya says she wants, more than anything, is to feel normal in her own car again. She says this quietly, almost apologetically, as if it is too small a thing to ask for. It is not a small thing. It is, in fact, everything she has lost.
